mcqs.question: Why did SATA/AHCI's protocol overhead only become a real bottleneck once SSDs became common?
options: AHCI was never designed to work with SSDs at all and physically cannot connect to them
SSDs require more electrical power than AHCI can supply

When HDDs dominated, multi-millisecond mechanical latency dwarfed the protocol's microsecond-scale overhead; once flash access dropped to microseconds, that same overhead became significant relative to the device itself
AHCI was specifically designed to intentionally throttle SSD performance
mcqs.explanation: The bottleneck shift is about relative overhead: protocol cost that was negligible against HDD latency becomes significant against SSD latency. AHCI does work with SSDs (just suboptimally), and power supply and intentional throttling aren't the actual causes.

mcqs.question: Why does NVMe support tens of thousands of command queues instead of AHCI's single queue?
options: To allow the SSD to connect to more physical devices simultaneously
Because each queue corresponds to a different file on the filesystem
Because more queues automatically reduce the SSD's power consumption

Because an SSD's internal flash has many independent channels/dies capable of genuine parallel service, and multiple queues let software keep that internal hardware parallelism busy instead of funneling everything through one bottleneck
mcqs.explanation: Multiple queues exist to match software-side request parallelism to the SSD's genuine internal hardware parallelism. Queue count isn't about connecting more physical devices, isn't a power-saving mechanism, and has no relationship to individual files.

mcqs.question: For which scenario would the SATA/AHCI vs NVMe distinction matter the least?
options: A single, older mechanical HDD where access latency is dominated by seek time and rotational latency, not protocol overhead
A high-performance NVMe SSD serving many concurrent random I/O requests from a database
A datacenter array of the fastest available flash drives under heavy concurrent load
Any workload issuing sustained, high queue-depth random I/O
mcqs.explanation: On a mechanical HDD, mechanical latency dominates so thoroughly that protocol queue depth/overhead differences barely register. The other scenarios all involve fast devices and/or high concurrency, exactly where NVMe's advantages become significant.

mcqs.question: Why is it inaccurate to describe NVMe as 'a type of connector' the way SATA is often loosely described?
options: NVMe drives never use any physical connector at all

NVMe is a protocol (a command set and queueing model) that most commonly runs over PCIe, but can also run over a network as NVMe-oF — describing it as a connector hides that it isn't tied to one physical interface
NVMe and PCIe are simply two names for the exact same standard
NVMe only exists as a theoretical specification with no real hardware implementations
mcqs.explanation: NVMe is defined as a protocol independent of its physical carrier, which is exactly why NVMe-oF (over Ethernet, Fibre Channel, etc.) can exist. NVMe drives do use physical connectors (M.2, U.2), NVMe and PCIe are distinct standards, and NVMe has widespread real hardware implementations.

mcqs.question: Why does NVMe's throughput advantage over AHCI grow as CPU core count increases?
options: Each core can own its own submission/completion queue pair with no shared-lock contention, unlike AHCI's single queue shared by every core
NVMe automatically overclocks the storage device when more cores are available
AHCI becomes physically incompatible with systems that have more than one core
More cores make the PCIe link itself run at a higher clock speed
mcqs.explanation: NVMe lets the OS assign one queue pair per core, so cores issue and complete I/O independently with no shared-structure contention. AHCI's single shared queue means every core issuing I/O contends on the same structure, a bottleneck that gets worse as more cores try to use it concurrently -- it has nothing to do with clock speed or compatibility.

mcqs.question: An NVMe SSD is rated at 500K IOPS, but a workload issuing one command at a time (queue depth 1) sees far less. Why?
options: The rated figure assumes many commands in flight simultaneously; at queue depth 1, per-command latency isn't overlapped and throughput is bounded by that single latency
The device is defective if it doesn't hit 500K IOPS at any queue depth
Queue depth only affects sequential workloads, never random IOPS
NVMe requires a minimum of 500K outstanding commands to function at all
mcqs.explanation: Rated IOPS figures are measured at deep queue depths where many commands overlap their latency across the device's parallel flash channels. At queue depth 1, each command must finish before the next is issued, so throughput is bounded by 1/latency -- a small fraction of the rated number, not a sign of a defective device.
